page.text:
A mathematical theory is defined as much by the questions it cannot yet
answer as by the theorems it has successfully established. A conjecture
belongs in a foundational library only when its statement is
mathematically precise and its unproved status is unmistakable. The open
problems presented here are not isolated curiosities or recreational
puzzles; each arises organically from the foundational structures
developed throughout this volume, and each sits at the epicenter of
modern mathematical research.

These problems dramatically illustrate the insurmountable chasm
separating empirical verification from deductive proof. An assertion
about all integers or all complex zeros cannot be demonstrated by testing
billions or trillions of cases. The history of number theory is filled
with plausible conjectures supported by vast numerical evidence that
ultimately proved false—such as the Mertens conjecture, which was
verified for billions of values before being disproved by Andrew Odlyzko
and Herman te Riele in 1985, or the oscillation of
$\pi(x) - \operatorname{li}(x)$, which first changes sign only beyond
Skewes' astronomical numbers.

In an axiomatic library like **Mathlore**, conjecture cards serve a vital
architectural role: they state exact mathematical claims without
compromising deductive integrity, demarcating the precise frontier
between established truth and open exploration.
